newsitem.title: UK: World bond investors shun puny yields.
newsitem.headline: World bond investors shun puny yields.

text.p: Global bond market euphoria sent debt prices to record high levels last week, but as investors grow uneasy about the resulting low yields the risks of a correction are mounting, analysts said on Monday.
Changing expectations of European interest rates pushed benchmark Bund yields near to historic lows, while key technical levels were broken on most bond futures contracts.
"With (10-year) Bund yields at 5.6 percent, investors are reluctant to chase yields much lower," said Philip Tyson, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.
"The long end of Europe is going to find progress increasingly difficult," he said.
Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London, said German benchmark yields would hit resistance at 5.5 percent, as most investors left the market.

He said there would be market resistance to the yield on the benchmark U.S. long bond falling below 6.25 percent, compared with a current level of about 6.38 percent. Japanese bonds, too, were in uncharted territory with a record low 182nd bond yield of 2.35 percent.
"This will be a crucial week for the global rally," said Knuthsen. "If the U.S. non-farm payrolls and the German gdp are slightly too strong there could be a correction."
German third quarter GDP figures were due for release on Wednesday, and U.S. November non-farm payrolls data on Friday.
Analysts said the recent rise in bond prices has been too sharp to be categorised simply as a traditional year-end rally.

"Until last week, the market thought German rates were on hold for the forseeable future," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "There was a shift to thinking that rates could come down a bit further to aid growth and keep the EMU bandwagon rolling."

But he said further potential for a fall in German interest rates was limited, as they were already at historic lows. The repo rate is at five percent, while the lombard and discount rates are at 4.5 percent and 2.5 percent respectively.
Analysts said the Bundesbank was unlikely to cave in to pressure from Bank of France officials to cut interest rates.

"The Bundesbank will probably pursue the route of hinting at rate cuts and a stronger dollar and generally talking expectations up," said Wattret. "But the GDP figures, coupled with strong M3 will not really be conducive to a rate cut."
He said the numbers could trigger a bond market correction.
Sheltering from a bond market storm could prove difficult, analysts said, as most markets have been caught up in the move.

Analysts said British gilts, which have underperformed, are risky in the short term, with some expectations of a quarter percentage point rise in British base rates in the first three months of 1997. Base rates are currently at six percent.
"On a six to 12 month view, gilts look attractive," said Wattret. "It could be one of the markets hit least hard."
